assessment.name: AT1: Viva Voce
assessment.detail: A Viva Voce with an aural focus and a short performance checkpoint. Presented live, recorded or written, student's choice. Full task and rubric are in Canvas.

outcomesReferenced: describes the ways Music context and Music language shape music
uses aural skills to identify and describe features of music
interprets and communicates musical ideas in performance
performs repertoire with stylistic awareness and technical control
uses Compositional language to create musical ideas
applies Music context and Music language to realise musical intent in composition

lessons.title: Style, genre and conventions
lessons.intention: Define style, genre and musical conventions, and tell them apart. Name conventions you can hear in a work and say what era, place or culture they point to.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Name the style and genre of a work, point to two conventions you can hear, and explain one way its context shapes the sound, using correct terminology.
lessons.listeningNote: Also meet M 02 Oye Como Va, M 03 Libertango and M 04 Chan Chan across these two weeks: one frame held against three different global traditions.
steps: Diagnostic listening: jot what you notice about a short excerpt, with no labels yet.
Compare contrasting works, for example a 12-bar blues, an Australian pop song, and a work from a non-Western tradition chosen with cultural protocols.
For each, name the style and genre, then list two conventions you can hear.
Add the new terms to your unit glossary.
criteria: Name the style and genre of a work.
Point to two conventions you can hear.
Explain one way context shapes the sound, using correct terminology.

blocks.brief: Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, first movement: Classical-era serenade, sonata-form conventions on full display.
Tito Puente's Oye Como Va: same three ideas (style, genre, convention), a completely different tradition.
Astor Piazzolla's Libertango: tango nuevo from Argentina, a third tradition against the same frame. The driving ostinato and the bandoneón are the conventions to name.
Buena Vista Social Club's Chan Chan: Cuban son, and the fourth work in the set. Set its conventions beside the Argentinian tango above and say what separates them.

blocks.title: The three ideas inside "Music context"
columns: A question to ask of a work
rows: The characteristic manner in which music is composed, performed or understood.
What makes this sound like the thing it is?
A category of music based on formal and cultural criteria.
What family of music does this belong to?
The established practices, norms and rules that govern a genre, culture or period.

blocks.title: Worked example: hearing conventions
blocks.text: Take a 12-bar blues. The conventions you can point to include a repeating 12-bar chord pattern built on chords I, IV and V, a swung rhythmic feel, blue notes in the melody, and a call-and-response shape between voice and instrument. Those conventions are what make it recognisable as blues rather than, say, a march or a pop ballad.

lessons.title: Compositional devices
lessons.intention: Identify rhythmic, melodic, textural and structural compositional devices in repertoire, and explain the effect a device has on the music.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Name a device by ear, use the correct term, and explain its effect in one clear sentence.
steps: Listen to a short excerpt twice.
Name one device you can hear and write the timestamp.
In one sentence, explain its effect (for example, "the ostinato builds tension because it never resolves").
Swap with a partner and check you agree on the term.
criteria: Name a device by ear.
Use the correct term.
Explain its effect in one clear sentence.

blocks.brief: Bill Withers' Ain't No Sunshine: listen for the compositional devices (ostinato bass, the wordless "I know" repetitions as a built-in device, not an ad-lib).

blocks.title: Compositional language by family
rows: ostinato, syncopation, swing, backbeat, groove, triplets
Drives the music and gives it feel.
Shapes the tune and makes it memorable.
Controls how many layers you hear and how they combine.
motif, theme, verse–chorus, call and response, binary, ternary

blocks.title: Listen for these four first
rows: A short pattern repeated through a passage.
A riff or rhythm that keeps coming back unchanged.
Accents placed off the main beat.
The push or surprise when a note lands between beats.
A short, catchy repeated melodic or rhythmic idea.
A guitar or keyboard hook that anchors the song.
A melodic idea repeated higher or lower.
The same shape moving up or down in steps.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Aural identification is done from excerpts your teacher selects in class. The Canvas quiz for this topic tests the terminology and the effect of each device.

lessons.title: Tonality by ear: pentatonic, major, minor, Aeolian
lessons.intention: Recognise pentatonic, major, minor and Aeolian tonality by ear, sing and play these scales on a keyboard, and describe what you hear that tells you the tonality.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Hear major versus minor reliably, identify pentatonic and Aeolian, and say what you heard that told you.
lessons.listeningNote: Chosen for this lesson because its verse and chorus sit in different tonalities: good ear-training for telling major from minor inside one song.
steps: Play C major, then C minor on keyboard. Name the note that changed (the third).
Play the black keys only to hear a pentatonic scale.
Play A to A on white keys to hear Aeolian.
Sing each scale up and down, then identify a teacher-played example by ear.
criteria: Hear major versus minor reliably.
Identify pentatonic and Aeolian.
Say what you heard that told you.

blocks.brief: Fleetwood Mac's Dreams: verse and chorus sit in different tonalities; listen for the shift by ear before naming it.

blocks.title: Four tonalities to know this term
rows: Five notes, no semitone clashes (for example C D E G A).
Open, folk-like, easy on the ear.
Tunes that sound like they fit the black keys.
A confident, 'happy' resolution to the tonic.
A lowered third compared with major.
The natural minor mode (white notes A to A).
Minor but plain, no raised leading note.
A minor feel with a flat seventh, common in folk and pop.

blocks.title: Tell major from minor first
blocks.text: Start by deciding bright or dark. The clue is the third degree of the scale. A major third sounds bright and open; a minor third sounds darker. Once you hear minor, check the seventh: if the note below the tonic is a whole tone away (a flat seventh), you are likely hearing Aeolian rather than harmonic minor.

blocks.title: Where this fits
blocks.text: This is the first step of the Year 11 aural progression. Contexts of music covers pentatonic, major, minor and Aeolian. Dorian, Lydian and Mixolydian come later, in the Creative practice unit.

lessons.title: Harmony by ear: chords I, IV, V and vi
lessons.intention: Identify chords I, IV, V and vi by ear in songs, play simple progressions on keyboard or guitar, and explain how the chords support the melody and mood.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Find the tonic, hear a move to IV, V or vi, and play a I–V–vi–IV progression.
lessons.listeningNote: No work from the register is pinned to this lesson; a teacher-chosen song carries the identification activity in class.
steps: Find the tonic (I). Hum the note that feels like home.
When the chord changes, ask: does it feel like it is moving away (IV), pulling back home (V), or going darker (vi)?
Play the bass note: the lowest note often names the chord.
Test your guess by playing the progression on a keyboard, then identify it in a teacher-chosen song by ear.
criteria: Find the tonic.
Hear a move to IV, V or vi.
Play a I–V–vi–IV progression.

blocks.title: The four chords that power most songs
rows: Major: a step away from home.
Major: wants to pull back to I.
Minor: the relative minor, adds colour.

blocks.title: Where this fits
blocks.text: Chords ii and V7 belong to the next focus area (Creative practice). Stay with I, IV, V and vi for now.

lessons.title: Motifs and development in the DAW
lessons.intention: Create a short motif using Compositional language, develop it with rhythmic, melodic and harmonic devices, and document each stage of your idea in the DAW.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Create a short motif, develop it with at least one named device, and document the change in your DAW.
lessons.listeningNote: A creating lesson, not a listening one. GarageBand on the iPads or Flat.io for notation.
steps: Week 2: improvise and capture a short motif that reflects a chosen tradition.
Week 4: extend the motif using rhythmic and melodic devices.
Week 8: add a simple I, IV, V, vi progression under the motif.
Week 10: get feedback, refine, and export an audio file.
criteria: Create a short motif.
Develop it with at least one named device.
Document the change in your DAW.

blocks.title: Ways to develop a motif
rows: Add syncopation, turn it into an ostinato, or augment the note values.
Move it up or down as a sequence, invert it, or turn it into a riff.
Add a countermelody, double it an octave up, or loop it.
Place it over I, IV, V or vi and hear how the mood changes.

blocks.title: Documenting is assessable practice
blocks.text: For each sketch, save a new version and write one or two lines: what the idea is, what device you used, and what you will try next. This habit feeds directly into the Year 11 composition development requirements.

blocks.title: Using First Nations material in your work
blocks.text: If you want to build on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander musical material in a sketch, talk to your teacher before you start. Some material is sacred or restricted and is not yours to sample, imitate or rework.

lessons.title: Interpreting music in context
lessons.intention: Explain how context influences the way a work is interpreted, compare two versions of the same work and account for the differences, and investigate how performance conventions carry stylistic identity.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Compare two versions of a work, name what changed, and explain how context accounts for the difference, with musical evidence.
lessons.listeningNote: Heard with its Community and its context present, never played cold for marks. It is not used in the AT3 examination.
steps: Compare an original recording with a later cover of the same song, using the original-versus-cover frame.
Investigate performance conventions across two traditions and note how their conventions reflect distinct contexts.
Week 9: write a short, evidence-based paragraph analysing how context shapes meaning in one chosen work, using identify, describe, explain.
Support each point in your paragraph with a specific musical example.
criteria: Compare two versions of a work.
Name what changed.
Explain how context accounts for the difference, with musical evidence.

blocks.brief: Archie Roach's Took the Children Away: heard with its context first, never played cold for marks.

blocks.title: From exploring to interpreting
blocks.text: In the first half of the term you explored how context shapes music. Now you turn to interpretation: how performers and audiences make meaning from a work, and how that meaning shifts with context.

blocks.title: Adjustment
blocks.text: A paragraph scaffold and a reduced-language-load version are available for students who need them.

lessons.title: Performance: technique and expression for style
lessons.intention: Perform using techniques appropriate to the style and genre, shape a performance with dynamics, articulation and phrasing, and adjust your playing in response to feedback.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Perform a short piece with technique that suits the style, make one clear expressive choice, and act on feedback.
lessons.listeningNote: A performing lesson: you are the listening example. These workshops also rehearse your AT1 performance checkpoint.
steps: Week 2: technique for style, clean and controlled playing that fits the idiom.
Week 4: expression through dynamics, articulation and phrasing.
Logbook entry each workshop: what you performed, one technique or expressive choice you worked on, feedback received, one goal for next time.
Keep your logbook current; it is your evidence of progress toward AT1.
criteria: Perform a short piece with technique that suits the style.
Make one clear expressive choice.
Act on feedback.

blocks.title: Expressive devices toolkit
rows: How loud or soft (p, f, crescendo, diminuendo).
Grow louder into a phrase peak, then ease back.
How notes are attacked and joined (staccato, legato, accent).
Play a phrase staccato, then legato; hear the change.
Breathe or lift at the end of each phrase.
Colour added to a sustained note or timbre.
Add a little vibrato on long notes where the style allows.

lessons.title: Technologies and the development of styles
lessons.intention: Explain how recording and production technologies shaped a style, compare contrasting eras of the same style, and use production terms accurately.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Name a technology, point to where you hear its effect, and explain how it shaped the style.
lessons.listeningNote: Listening examples chosen in class: an early, lightly produced recording against a later, heavily produced one in the same style.
steps: Listen to an early, lightly produced recording in a style.
Listen to a later, heavily produced recording in the same style.
List three differences you can hear and link each to a technology.
Explain how the technology changed the listener experience.
criteria: Name a technology.
Point to where you hear its effect.
Explain how it shaped the style.

blocks.title: Technology is part of the story of a style
blocks.text: Styles do not develop in a vacuum. The tools available to record, produce and distribute music have shaped how it sounds. Multitrack recording, electric instruments, sampling and the DAW each changed what was possible.

blocks.title: Technologies and what they allowed
rows: Studio pop and rock from the 1960s on.
Composing, editing and producing on a computer.

blocks.title: Production terms to use
blocks.text: Looping, sampling, delay, echo, pitch shifting, digital reverb, electroacoustic, waveform, piano roll, beat grid.

lessons.title: Notation in context: lead sheets, tab, drum and staff
lessons.intention: Read and interpret lead sheets, tablature, drum notation and staff notation, match the notation type to the repertoire and tradition, and transcribe a short idea into an appropriate notation.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Read each notation type, say where it is used, and transcribe a short idea into a suitable form.
lessons.listeningNote: Listening and transcription happen in class, from a short riff in your own repertoire.
steps: Choose a short riff from your repertoire.
Write it in two forms: staff notation and one other (tab or drum notation).
Swap with a partner and play each other's transcriptions.
criteria: Read each notation type.
Say where it is used.
Transcribe a short idea into a suitable form.

blocks.title: Notation represents Music language in different ways
rows: Which fret and string to play.
Which drum or cymbal and when.
Waveform, piano roll or beat grid.

blocks.title: Reading a lead sheet
blocks.text: Read the chord symbols above the stave (for example C, F, G, Am) as you follow the melody. The symbols tell you the harmony; the notes give the tune; the lyrics align underneath.

lessons.title: Aural and theory drills: metre, tempo and rhythm
lessons.intention: Hear and notate simple and compound metre, identify tempo and changes in tempo, and recognise and write down common rhythmic patterns.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Tell simple from compound metre, name the tempo, and notate a short rhythm you hear.
lessons.listeningNote: Aural skill grows with short, regular practice. Most lessons open with this 10-minute drill; this page is the reference for the rhythm and metre content running through the term.
steps: Listen and decide: simple or compound metre?
Tap the beat and name the tempo.
Clap back a two-bar pattern, then notate it.
Self-check against the answer your teacher shows.
criteria: Tell simple from compound metre.
Name the tempo.
Notate a short rhythm you hear.

blocks.title: Metre: simple versus compound
rows: Three (e.g. dotted crotchet into three quavers).

blocks.title: Where this fits
blocks.text: Use this page across Weeks 1, 6 and 10. The Week 10 consolidation drill mixes all of the above.

lessons.title: Unit review and vocabulary check
lessons.intention: Pull the whole term together. Revisit Music context and Music language, check the term's vocabulary against your own glossary, and put those words into a well-formed dot point, which is the writing shape the rest of this course is built on.
lessons.whatYouWillDo: Use this term's vocabulary correctly in the cumulative review quiz, and write a well-formed dot point about a work you have studied: the feature named, the evidence you heard, and the effect it has.
lessons.listeningNote: Excerpts are drawn from works already studied this term and chosen on the day. A review lesson introduces nothing new.
steps: Cumulative review quiz, twelve questions across the whole term: Music context and Music language, rhythmic and melodic devices, tonality and harmony by ear, metre, notation types and production techniques.
Glossary audit. Work back through the unit glossary you have been building since Week 1. Any term you cannot define in your own words gets rewritten, in your own words, before Term 2.
Listening recall: short excerpts from works already studied, named cold. For each, give the style, one convention you can hear, and one Music language feature.
Write one well-formed dot point on a work from this term, then swap and check a partner's against the same three parts.
Name one thing from Contexts of music you expect to carry into Creative practice next term.
criteria: Use this term's vocabulary correctly in the review quiz.
Name the style, one convention and one Music language feature in an excerpt you have already studied.
Write a well-formed dot point that names a feature, gives the evidence you heard, and states its effect.

blocks.title: The term's vocabulary, and where you met it
columns: Terms you should be able to define without help
rows: Pentatonic, major, minor, Aeolian (the natural minor)
Chords I, IV, V and vi; the I-V-vi-IV progression
Staff notation, lead sheet, tablature, drum notation
Simple metre, compound metre (6/8), tempo markings

blocks.title: Worked example: a well-formed dot point
blocks.text: A well-formed dot point has three parts and fits on one line: the feature you are talking about, the evidence you actually heard, and the effect it has. One element per dot point, and never a paragraph. Take Bill Withers' Ain't No Sunshine from Lesson 2. A weak answer says the song is sad, which names no feature and gives no evidence. A well-formed one says: the vocal line is built on one short repeated idea, and in the middle section the lyric drops away to a single phrase repeated over the same accompaniment, which holds the listener on one thought instead of moving the story on. Feature, evidence, effect. This is the shape every listening answer takes from here to the end of Year 12, so it is worth getting automatic now rather than in the week before an examination.

blocks.title: The review quiz
blocks.text: Twelve questions, one mark each, covering the whole of Contexts of music. It is a check on where your vocabulary actually is, not an assessment task: Assessment Task 1 was Week 8 and nothing here is weighted. Use the result to decide what goes back into your glossary over the break.
